Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents' is a hard-to-explain trigger because it implies a transport/accident trauma context rather than disaster-related cues. This is not just unusual; it mismatches the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The Threat node includes 'Flashbacks', which is more a re-experiencing/memory phenomenon than a current threat belief or arousal cue. Given that Memory is structurally isolated in the formulation, placing a prominent memory-like item in Threat creates a formulation mismatch, especially when no Memory items are endorsed to support that link.

The trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. 'Being seen' and 'feeling watched or observed' imply an interpersonal/social-threat cue set rather than reminders of an impersonal disaster. With no memory items or appraisals referencing social judgment, persecution, or assault, these two trigger items look clinically mismatched to the trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals 'I am inadequate' and 'I can't rely on myself' can occur after trauma, but in this profile they pair mainly with social-observation triggers and do not connect clearly to a natural-disaster formulation. The remaining items emphasize generalized threat/hypervigilance, whereas these appraisals suggest a more interpersonal/shame-based presentation. That makes the profile as a whole less coherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'feeling watched or observed' is difficult to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger. It suggests interpersonal persecution/surveillance rather than an environmental disaster cue, while the other trigger items are disaster-congruent.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: 'Scanning exits' is not impossible, but paired with a natural-disaster trauma and the other selected items it points toward man-made/interpersonal danger in enclosed spaces rather than the presented disaster context. This makes the threat profile feel partially mismatched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate
issues.explanation: The negative-appraisal set is otherwise about global damage and reduced self-reliance after trauma. 'I am inadequate' can occur in PTSD, but here it reads as a generalized self-worth theme without a clear link to the disaster-based trigger/threat pattern, making the appraisal node somewhat less coherent than the other two items.

vignette:
The storm surge had come inland so fast that there was no time to run, only time to climb. At twenty years old, Amara had been visiting her parents' coastal village during a brief break from medical school, and she remembered the exact moment the wall of water shattered the front door-the sound of wood splintering like bone, the way the brown water rose past her calves, her hips, her chest, before she managed to pull herself onto the roof beams. She held onto a rafter for what felt like hours, listening to the screams of neighbors she had known since childhood, feeling the house tremble and groan beneath her, certain that at any moment the beam would give way and she would be swept into the darkness. She survived, but the water had taken her younger brother, who had been visiting from the city and had been standing just three feet from her when the surge hit. She had reached for him, and her hand had closed on nothing.

In the months that followed, Amara threw herself back into her surgical residency with a ferocity that her attending physicians praised as dedication. They did not see what she saw when she closed her eyes at night: the brown water, the splintering wood, the empty space where her brother's hand should have been. She stopped going to the hospital gym because the rhythmic pounding of her feet on the treadmill sounded too much like the water slamming against the roof. She told herself she was simply too tired from long shifts, but the truth was that her heart would begin to race the moment she stepped onto the tread, her chest tightening until she could not breathe, and she would have to sit down on the floor with her head between her knees until the feeling passed.

The weather became an enemy she could not escape. On the first rainy morning of autumn, Amara walked into the operating room and saw the sky through the window-low, gray, swollen with moisture-and her hands began to shake so violently that the scrub nurse asked if she was ill. She said she was fine, and she forced her hands to steady, but inside she was already back on that beam, feeling the wind pick up, hearing the water rise. She began checking the forecast obsessively, multiple times a day, and on days when the barometric pressure dropped, she found herself canceling social plans, calling in sick, lying in her apartment with every light on because the darkness felt like the water closing over her head. She had come to believe that she could not rely on herself anymore-that her own body would betray her at any moment, that she was fundamentally broken in a way that surgery could not fix. What frightened her most was the certainty that bad things would keep happening, that she could not stop them, that the universe had singled her out for destruction and was simply waiting for the next opportunity.

In the operating room, she became hypervigilant in a way that her colleagues mistook for thoroughness. She checked and rechecked instruments, read patient charts three times, startled at the clatter of a dropped scalpel. She jumped at the sound of a door slamming in the hallway, at the sudden beep of a monitor, at the crash cart being wheeled past. Every unexpected noise sent a jolt through her body, and she could feel her pulse in her throat, her palms slick with sweat, her vision narrowing as if she were preparing to fight or flee-though there was nothing to fight, nothing to flee from except the memory that lived inside her own skull. She tried to control her emotions by sheer force of will, keeping her face neutral, her voice even, her movements precise. But the control cost her everything. When a senior surgeon criticized her technique, she nodded meekly, apologized, agreed with every word, even when she knew she was right. She had become overly compliant, unable to assert herself, certain that any disagreement would bring punishment or abandonment. Her colleagues began to notice that Amara, once outspoken and confident, now said yes to everything, took on extra shifts she did not want, accepted blame for mistakes that were not hers.

Her life had been destroyed, she was certain of that. Not just her brother's death, but the person she had been before the water came. She no longer recognized herself. She could not sleep without a lamp on, and when she woke in the dark-which she did, night after night, gasping, disoriented, her hands clawing at the sheets-she would lie still, listening for the sound of water, waiting for the floor to flood. She came to therapy because a colleague found her crying in the supply closet, unable to explain why, unable to stop. Amara said she wanted to stop being afraid of the rain. She did not say that what she really wanted was to stop being afraid of herself.
